title: Sea Otters in Kelp

before.title: Why Otters Hold Hands
before.text: Sea otters often rest on the water. Waves and wind can move them apart. Sometimes two otters hold paws while they float. A group may also rest among sea plants. The plants help keep them in one place. Holding on does not happen every time, but it can help partners stay close while they sleep. The sea is always moving. Staying close can help the group feel safe and find one another when they wake.

after.title: Sea Otters in Kelp
after.text: Sea otters spend much of their day floating and looking for food near kelp forests. They also live in coves and bays. An otter may dive to the seafloor for crabs or clams. Then it returns to the surface to eat. It floats on its back and uses its chest like a table. It may use a rock to open a hard shell.

reason: The earlier title and ending treated paw-holding as a documented way to stay close and feel safe, but the checked institutional source did not support that causal claim. Replace it with documented habitat, diving, surface feeding and rock use.

title: The Inca Road Network

before.title: A Road Across the Andes
before.text: The Inca built roads across high mountains in South America. People carried messages by running from one station to the next. They did not use horses or carts on these roads. Rope bridges crossed deep low land between mountains. The great road system joined farms, towns, and large rooms that held food. A runner gave each message to a new runner, so news could move far. Parts of the old roads remain today.

after.title: The Inca Road Network
after.text: The Inca road network crossed mountains, valleys, forests, and deserts in the Andes. It linked towns and important centers over long distances. Messengers, travelers, armies, and groups of people used the roads. Builders adapted the network to difficult land. They made bridges, stairs, ditches, and stone paths where needed. Buildings beside the roads provided places for storage and rest. Parts of this large network remain today.

reason: Remove unsupported details about relay stations, the absence of horses and carts, and vague “deep low land.” Retain UNESCO-supported scale, users, terrain, bridges, stairs, ditches, paving, storage and accommodation in accessible Level 2 prose.

title: Why a Spoon Looks Bent

before.title: A Spoon Looks Bent
before.text: Put a spoon in a clear glass of water. From the side, it may look bent. Light moves through air and water at different speeds. Its path changes at the surface of the water. Your eyes follow the changed light, so the spoon seems to be in a new place. It is still straight. The light, not the metal, has changed its path.

after.title: Why a Spoon Looks Bent
after.text: Put a straight spoon in a clear glass of water. From the side, it may look bent where it enters the water. Light changes speed when it passes between water and air. Its direction can change at that boundary. This change is called refraction. The light reaches your eyes along a changed path. The part under the water then seems to be in a different place. The spoon itself is still straight.

reason: Name refraction and connect the apparent position to light changing direction at the water-air boundary. The statement is limited to the observation and mechanism described by the checked open physics text.

title: How a Sonoran Desert Tortoise Stores Water

before.title: Water Saved by a Tortoise
before.text:
A desert tortoise lives in a dry place. It spends time in a home under the ground, away from great heat.

After rain, it can drink and store water in its body. This stored water matters when little water is available.

People should watch wild tortoises from a distance. Picking one up can disturb it and cause it to lose stored water.

after.title: How a Sonoran Desert Tortoise Stores Water
after.text: A Sonoran desert tortoise lives where rain can be rare. It may spend dry periods in a burrow. When water is available, the tortoise can drink a large amount. Its bladder can store water and later return some of that water to the blood. This helps the tortoise during a short or seasonal drought. The stored water also helps its body handle salts and waste. These facts describe the Sonoran desert tortoise, not every tortoise species.

reason: Specify the Sonoran desert tortoise and replace the broad phrase “store water in its body” with the documented bladder function. Remove handling advice from an explanatory physiology passage and explicitly limit the species scope.
